"Kunal, everyone's asking. Chacha says it's for the family's name," Samir said.

"I know they care. I'm just not ready to sit at one table with my brother yet."

"It's been two years."

"And after what happened at his house, I don't feel safe alone with him."

Samir was quiet a moment. "What if someone neutral sat between you? Someone the family trusts, like the counsellor from the temple committee?"

"A mediator I might do. Someone neutral, in a public place, with the door open."

"And the date?"

"Mine. Not wedding season."

"I'll tell them."

"Tell them I'm not the villain either."

"Nobody said that."

"Everybody's faces did."

qa.q: Where does Kunal want any meeting with the mediator to take place?
qa.a: In a public place, with the door open.

qa.q: What does Kunal mean by "Everybody's faces did"?
qa.a: Kunal feels hurt and judged: though nobody said it, the relatives' looks cast Kunal as the villain.

qa.q: What conditions did Kunal set for peace talks?
qa.a: A neutral mediator, a public place with the door open, and a date Kunal chooses outside wedding season.

qa.q: Why might Samir keep raising the subject?
qa.a: Samir carries the relatives' care for the family, though Samir listens to Kunal's limits and offers the mediator idea.

grounding: Relatives push the protagonist to make peace for appearances; the protagonist listens, keeps their own timing, may accept a neutral mediator and protects safety.

"Leela, beta, it has been two years. People at the temple are asking why you never come to your father's house."
"I know, Pallavi Mami. Thank you for coming all this way."
"Just come for Navratri. One evening. For the family's name."
"I hear that you're worried about all of us. I really do." Leela poured the tea and kept her voice steady. "But I'm not walking back into that house, after what happened last time, because of what people at the temple say."
"So you'll never make peace?"
"I didn't say never. If Papa wants to talk, I'll do it with someone neutral in the room. Dr Rao at the community centre has done this for other families."
"A stranger? Between father and daughter?"
"Someone who isn't on anyone's side. And on my timing, Mami. Not before Navratri just so the photos look nice."
Mami set down her cup. "I'll tell him. He won't like it."
"That's alright. I'll be here."

qa.q: What did Pallavi Mami ask Leela to do?
qa.a: Come for Navratri, one evening, for the family's name.

qa.q: How can you tell Leela feels both cared for and firm?
qa.a: She thanks Mami and says she hears the worry, yet keeps her voice steady and refuses to go for appearances; she feels touched but determined.

qa.q: What option does Leela offer instead of going to the house?
qa.a: Talking with Papa only with a neutral person present, such as Dr Rao from the community centre, and on her own timing.

qa.q: What is it like for Pallavi Mami when Leela suggests a stranger?
qa.a: Mami is surprised and uneasy, since a stranger between father and daughter feels odd, yet she agrees to carry the message.

grounding: Relatives press the protagonist to reconcile for the family name; she listens to their care but keeps her own timing and accepts only a neutral mediator.

passage:
A year ago the family group chat turned into a campaign. My cousin Himani sent a long voice note every morning: "Bhupen, Dada is getting old, he wants both grandsons at his table. Do it for the family." I'm Bhupen, the one who stopped answering calls after my brother shoved me down the stairs at Dada's house during an argument.
Looking back, I'm glad I didn't snap at Himani. I told her, "I know you want everyone together, and I love you for that. But I won't sit across from him because the neighbours talk."
What I did agree to, months later, was one meeting in a counsellor's office that Himani found, with the counsellor between us and my own car parked outside. It went badly, honestly. But it happened on my terms, and I left when I needed to.

qa.q: What did Himani send every morning?
qa.a: A long voice note asking Bhupen to make peace for the family.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel about Himani's pressure, looking back?
qa.a: Bhupen feels grateful and fond of Himani's care yet still wary, glad not to have snapped but unwilling to face the brother just because neighbours talk.

qa.q: Which choice kept Bhupen safe while still giving peace a chance?
qa.a: Agreeing to one meeting in a counsellor's office, with the counsellor present and a car outside, so Bhupen could leave when needed.

qa.q: How might Himani see Bhupen's refusal at first?
qa.a: Himani may feel frustrated and worried about Dada's wish, reading it as stubbornness until the danger from the brother is taken seriously.

grounding: Relatives push the protagonist to reconcile for appearances; the protagonist listens, sets the timing, and accepts only a mediated meeting that keeps them safe.
